--- title: "Univariate models" subtitle: "Stationarity, ARMA, SARIMA, ETS, Holt-Winters and a seasonal naive benchmark" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/setup.R") suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(tseries) # adf.test, jarque.bera.test library(urca) # ur.kpss library(uroot) # hegy.test library(lmtest) # coeftest library(FinTS) # ArchTest }) # Format a p-value for the text, including the relation sign ("= 0.0100", "< 2.2e-16") fmt_p <- function(p) { if (p < 2.2e-16) return("< 2.2e-16") if (p < 0.001) return(paste("=", format(p, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE))) paste("=", sprintf("%.4f", p)) } # KPSS statistics with the 5% critical value kpss_table <- function(x) { do.call(rbind, lapply(c("tau", "mu"), function(type) { t <- ur.kpss(x, type = type) data.frame( Specification = if (type == "tau") "Trend (tau)" else "Constant (mu)", Statistic = round(t@teststat, 4), `Critical value 5%` = t@cval[, "5pct"], check.names = FALSE ) })) } # ADF p-values for several lag orders (tseries reports p-values within [0.01, 0.99]) adf_lags <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 24) adf_table <- function(x) { data.frame( Lag = adf_lags, `p-value` = sapply(adf_lags, function(k) suppressWarnings(adf.test(x, k = k)$p.value)), check.names = FALSE ) } # HEGY statistics and p-values by frequency hegy_table <- function(x) { h <- hegy.test(x) data.frame( Statistic = names(h$statistics), Value = round(h$statistics, 3), `p-value` = round(h$pvalues, 4), check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL ) } ``` ::: The series is the US Industrial Production Total Index (IPB50001N, 2017 = 100, not seasonally adjusted), monthly from January 1990 to April 2025 (424 observations). ## Visual analysis ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} autoplot(ip_ts) + labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![US industrial production, total index](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-ip-level-1.png){#fig-ip-level width=768} ::: ::: The series has a strong upward trend between 1990 and 2008, so its mean is not constant, which is a first sign of non-stationarity. Two major shocks stand out: the collapse during the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the very sharp but short-lived drop during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The trend and the level shifts call for formal unit root testing. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggtsdisplay(ip_ts) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Series, ACF and PACF in levels](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-ip-acf-1.png){#fig-ip-acf width=768} ::: ::: The ACF decays very slowly and almost linearly, staying far above the significance bands: the classic pattern of a non-stationary (unit root) process. The PACF has a large spike at lag 1 and significant spikes at the seasonal lags 12 and 24. Visually, the series needs both a regular difference (for the trend) and a seasonal difference at lag 12. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggsubseriesplot(ip_ts) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Index (2017 = 100)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Seasonal subseries: one panel per month, blue line = monthly mean](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-subseries-1.png){#fig-subseries width=768} ::: ::: The monthly means differ: June and August have the highest average production, while April and July are lower. Unequal monthly means are visual evidence of a seasonal component, which motivates the HEGY test for seasonal unit roots. ## Stationarity tests in levels **KPSS** (null hypothesis: the series is stationary): ::: {#tbl-kpss-level .cell tbl-cap='KPSS test, series in levels'} ```{.r .cell-code} kpss_level <- kpss_table(ip_ts) kpss_level ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Specification | Statistic| Critical value 5%| |:-------------|---------:|-----------------:| |Trend (tau) | 1.2744| 0.146| |Constant (mu) | 5.3919| 0.463|
::: ::: In both specifications the statistic is far above the 5% critical value, so stationarity is rejected: the original series is non-stationary. **ADF** (null hypothesis: unit root) for several lag orders, and **Phillips-Perron**: ::: {#tbl-adf-level .cell tbl-cap='ADF p-values by lag order, series in levels'} ```{.r .cell-code} adf_level <- adf_table(ip_ts) pp_level <- PP.test(ip_ts) adf_level ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag| p-value| |---:|---------:| | 1| 0.5683393| | 2| 0.6622783| | 3| 0.6272126| | 4| 0.7368886| | 5| 0.8011204| | 12| 0.3178361| | 24| 0.5213919|
::: ::: All ADF p-values are well above 0.05, so the unit root cannot be rejected. The Phillips-Perron test gives p = 0.5592 and leads to the same conclusion. KPSS, ADF and PP all agree that the series is non-stationary in levels. ## Seasonality test (HEGY) ::: {#tbl-hegy-level .cell tbl-cap='HEGY test, series in levels'} ```{.r .cell-code} hegy_level <- hegy_table(ip_ts) hegy_level ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Statistic | Value| p-value| |:---------|-------:|-------:| |t_1 | -2.560| 0.0922| |t_2 | -4.297| 0.0000| |F_3:4 | 75.300| 0.0000| |F_5:6 | 33.981| 0.0000| |F_7:8 | 71.140| 0.0000| |F_9:10 | 16.980| 0.0000| |F_11:12 | 14.272| 0.0000| |F_2:12 | 180.495| 0.0000| |F_1:12 | 175.207| 0.0000|
::: ::: For `t_1` (zero frequency) p = 0.0922, above 0.05, which again points to an ordinary unit root (non-stationarity in levels). For all seasonal frequencies (`t_2` and the F-statistics) the p-values are close to zero, so seasonal unit roots are rejected. To stabilise the series and prepare it for SARIMA, a log transformation and a seasonal difference at lag 12 are applied. ## Transformations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ip_log <- log(ip_ts) ip_seasonal_diff <- diff(ip_log, lag = 12) ip_stationary <- diff(ip_seasonal_diff) hegy_sdiff <- hegy_table(ip_seasonal_diff) hegy_sdiff ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Statistic | Value| p-value| |:---------|-------:|-------:| |t_1 | -5.556| 0| |t_2 | -5.784| 0| |F_3:4 | 59.466| 0| |F_5:6 | 56.451| 0| |F_7:8 | 64.749| 0| |F_9:10 | 49.096| 0| |F_11:12 | 34.038| 0| |F_2:12 | 577.674| 0| |F_1:12 | 532.493| 0|
::: ::: After the log transformation and the seasonal difference, all HEGY statistics, including `t_1`, have p-values close to zero. A first difference is then added, and the tests are repeated on the final series (log, seasonal difference and first difference): ::: {#tbl-tests-stationary .cell tbl-cap='KPSS and ADF tests, stationary series'} ```{.r .cell-code} kpss_table(ip_stationary) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Specification | Statistic| Critical value 5%| |:-------------|---------:|-----------------:| |Trend (tau) | 0.0189| 0.146| |Constant (mu) | 0.0204| 0.463|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} adf_stationary <- adf_table(ip_stationary) pp_stationary <- PP.test(ip_stationary) adf_stationary ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag| p-value| |---:|-------:| | 1| 0.01| | 2| 0.01| | 3| 0.01| | 4| 0.01| | 5| 0.01| | 12| 0.01| | 24| 0.01|
::: ::: All ADF p-values are 0.01, the smallest value `adf.test()` reports (the true p-value is lower), and Phillips-Perron gives p = 0.0100. The unit root is strongly rejected: the transformed series is stationary. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} autoplot(ip_stationary) + labs(x = "Year", y = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Stationary series: log, seasonal difference and first difference](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-stationary-1.png){#fig-stationary width=768} ::: ::: The transformed series no longer trends and fluctuates around zero. Higher volatility in 2008 and 2020 reflects the crisis episodes, but mean reversion is now clear. ## Train / test split ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_total <- length(ip_ts) n_train <- floor(0.75 * n_total) ip_train <- window(ip_ts, end = time(ip_ts)[n_train]) ip_test <- window(ip_ts, start = time(ip_ts)[n_train + 1]) ip_train_log <- window(ip_log, end = time(ip_log)[n_train]) h <- length(ip_test) ``` ::: The first 75% of the sample (318 months, to Jun 2016) is used to estimate the models; the last 106 months (Jul 2016 to Apr 2025) are kept for out-of-sample evaluation. The forecast horizon `h` equals the length of the test set, so RMSE, MAE and MAPE can be computed on it. ## ARMA models on the stationary series ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_stationary <- length(ip_stationary) n_train_stationary <- floor(0.75 * n_stationary) ip_stationary_train <- window( ip_stationary, end = time(ip_stationary)[n_train_stationary] ) ggtsdisplay(ip_stationary_train) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Training part of the stationary series, ACF and PACF](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-arma-acf-1.png){#fig-arma-acf width=768} ::: ::: Short lags (1–4) are significant in both the ACF and PACF, which points to short-run AR and MA components. There are also large negative spikes at the seasonal lags 12 and 24, so a non-seasonal ARMA model will struggle to remove the autocorrelation at long lags. This is why several models are estimated and why SARIMA follows. ::: {#tbl-arma .cell tbl-cap='Candidate ARMA models on the stationary training series'} ```{.r .cell-code} arma_orders <- list(c(1, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 1), c(1, 0, 1), c(1, 0, 2), c(2, 0, 1)) arma_models <- lapply(arma_orders, function(o) Arima(ip_stationary_train, order = o)) arma_auto <- auto.arima(ip_stationary_train, seasonal = FALSE) arma_compare <- data.frame( Model = c(sapply(arma_orders, function(o) sprintf("ARMA(%d,%d)", o[1], o[3])), "auto.arima"), Specification = c(sapply(arma_models, function(m) as.character(m)), as.character(arma_auto)), AIC = round(c(sapply(arma_models, AIC), AIC(arma_auto)), 2), BIC = round(c(sapply(arma_models, BIC), BIC(arma_auto)), 2) ) arma_compare ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Model |Specification | AIC| BIC| |:----------|:-------------------------------|--------:|--------:| |ARMA(1,0) |ARIMA(1,0,0) with non-zero mean | -1973.33| -1962.14| |ARMA(0,1) |ARIMA(0,0,1) with non-zero mean | -1971.16| -1959.97| |ARMA(1,1) |ARIMA(1,0,1) with non-zero mean | -1992.43| -1977.51| |ARMA(1,2) |ARIMA(1,0,2) with non-zero mean | -2003.97| -1985.32| |ARMA(2,1) |ARIMA(2,0,1) with non-zero mean | -2000.17| -1981.52| |auto.arima |ARIMA(2,0,3) with zero mean | -2013.90| -1991.52|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} coeftest(arma_auto) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` z test of coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) ar1 -0.143774 0.101072 -1.4225 0.1548837 ar2 0.619986 0.102608 6.0423 1.520e-09 *** ma1 0.220640 0.105175 2.0978 0.0359194 * ma2 -0.431159 0.126300 -3.4138 0.0006407 *** ma3 0.287870 0.064547 4.4598 8.203e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: `auto.arima()` selects ARIMA(2,0,3) with zero mean with AIC = -2013.9 and BIC = -1991.52, the lowest values among the candidates. The coefficients ar2, ma2 and ma3 are significant at 1% and ma1 at 5%; ar1 is not significant on its own but is kept to preserve the AR(2) structure. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arma_lb <- checkresiduals(arma_auto) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ljung-Box test data: Residuals from ARIMA(2,0,3) with zero mean Q* = 63.166, df = 19, p-value = 1.209e-06 Model df: 5. Total lags used: 24 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residual diagnostics, ARMA model](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-arma-resid-1.png){#fig-arma-resid width=768} ::: ::: The Ljung-Box test gives p = 1.21e-06 (< 0.05), so the null hypothesis of independent residuals is rejected: the residuals are not white noise. The ACF confirms remaining autocorrelation at the seasonal lags 12 and 24. A non-seasonal ARMA model cannot capture the full dynamics of the series, which justifies moving to SARIMA. ## SARIMA ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_final <- auto.arima( ip_train_log, seasonal = TRUE, stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE ) sarima_final ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Series: ip_train_log ARIMA(3,1,0)(0,1,1)[12] Coefficients: ar1 ar2 ar3 sma1 0.0335 0.1736 0.2787 -0.6240 s.e. 0.0550 0.0545 0.0555 0.0459 sigma^2 = 6.284e-05: log likelihood = 1043.37 AIC=-2076.74 AICc=-2076.54 BIC=-2058.14 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} coeftest(sarima_final) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` z test of coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) ar1 0.033529 0.055041 0.6092 0.542411 ar2 0.173565 0.054485 3.1855 0.001445 ** ar3 0.278703 0.055527 5.0192 5.189e-07 *** sma1 -0.624025 0.045860 -13.6072 < 2.2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: `auto.arima()` selects ARIMA(3,1,0)(0,1,1)[12] on the log of the training data, with both a regular (d = 1) and a seasonal (D = 1) difference, as suggested by the analysis above. The fit improves considerably: AIC falls to -2076.74 (from -2013.9 for ARMA). ar2, ar3 and the seasonal MA term sma1 are highly significant (p < 0.01); ar1 is kept for the consistency of the AR(3) structure. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_lb <- checkresiduals(sarima_final) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ljung-Box test data: Residuals from ARIMA(3,1,0)(0,1,1)[12] Q* = 16.173, df = 20, p-value = 0.7059 Model df: 4. Total lags used: 24 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residual diagnostics, SARIMA model](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-sarima-resid-1.png){#fig-sarima-resid width=768} ::: ::: The Ljung-Box test gives p = 0.7059 (> 0.05): the residuals show no autocorrelation and behave like white noise. The seasonal MA term removed the correlation at lags 12 and 24, and the histogram is roughly symmetric. ### Further residual tests ::: {#tbl-sarima-tests .cell tbl-cap='Ljung-Box and ARCH tests on the SARIMA residuals'} ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_resid <- residuals(sarima_final) lb_lags <- c(1:5, 8, 12, 24) sarima_lb_table <- data.frame( Lag = lb_lags, `Ljung-Box p-value` = sapply(lb_lags, function(l) { Box.test(sarima_resid, lag = l, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value }), check.names = FALSE ) arch_lags <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12) sarima_arch_table <- data.frame( Lag = arch_lags, `ARCH p-value` = sapply(arch_lags, function(l) ArchTest(sarima_resid, lags = l)$p.value), check.names = FALSE ) sarima_jb <- jarque.bera.test(sarima_resid) sarima_lb_table ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag| Ljung-Box p-value| |---:|-----------------:| | 1| 0.9199917| | 2| 0.9918702| | 3| 0.9350804| | 4| 0.9727387| | 5| 0.9774096| | 8| 0.9858611| | 12| 0.9532487| | 24| 0.8817441|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_arch_table ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag| ARCH p-value| |---:|------------:| | 1| 0.0001993| | 2| 0.0009375| | 4| 0.0004027| | 8| 0.0015016| | 12| 0.0000771|
::: ::: 1. **Autocorrelation (Ljung-Box):** all p-values are high (minimum 0.882), so the residuals are independent and the dynamics have been captured. 2. **Normality (Jarque-Bera):** p < 2.2e-16 (< 0.05), so normality is rejected. This is explained by turning points and major shocks (the 2008 crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 shock). 3. **Heteroscedasticity (ARCH):** p-values below 0.05 show ARCH effects (volatility clustering): the error variance is not constant, with larger residuals during episodes of macroeconomic instability. The model is valid for the conditional mean and is used for forecasting. ### SARIMA forecast ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_forecast <- forecast(sarima_final, h = h + 36) # Back-transform from logs with a bias correction for the mean sigma2 <- mean(residuals(sarima_final)^2) bias_correction <- exp(0.5 * sigma2) sarima_real <- sarima_forecast sarima_real$mean <- bias_correction * exp(sarima_forecast$mean) sarima_real$lower <- bias_correction * exp(sarima_forecast$lower) sarima_real$upper <- bias_correction * exp(sarima_forecast$upper) sarima_real$x <- exp(sarima_forecast$x) autoplot(sarima_real) + autolayer(ip_test, series = "Test data") + labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![SARIMA forecast (back-transformed to index levels) against the test data](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-sarima-forecast-1.png){#fig-sarima-forecast width=768} ::: ::: 1. The bias correction exp(σ²/2) adjusts the back-transformed forecast for the log transformation. 2. The forecast (blue) follows the centre of the test data (2016–2025) closely, which indicates good out-of-sample performance. 3. The 2020 COVID-19 shock appears as a large exogenous deviation; the data later return to the forecast path. 4. The uncertainty fan (2025–2028) widens asymmetrically, as expected for long-horizon macroeconomic forecasts on a log scale. ## Exponential smoothing (ETS) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ets_auto <- ets(ip_train, model = "ZZZ") ets_auto ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ETS(M,Ad,M) Call: ets(y = ip_train, model = "ZZZ") Smoothing parameters: alpha = 0.829 beta = 0.1046 gamma = 0.171 phi = 0.9789 Initial states: l = 61.6079 b = 0.0514 s = 0.9875 1 1.0138 1.0152 1.0081 0.9744 1.0172 0.9931 0.9909 1.0064 1.0037 0.9898 sigma: 0.0087 AIC AICc BIC 1666.886 1669.174 1734.603 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ets_lb <- checkresiduals(ets_auto) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ljung-Box test data: Residuals from ETS(M,Ad,M) Q* = 87.962, df = 24, p-value = 3.126e-09 Model df: 0. Total lags used: 24 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residual diagnostics, ETS model](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-ets-resid-1.png){#fig-ets-resid width=768} ::: ::: The automatic selection gives ETS(M,Ad,M): multiplicative errors, an additive damped trend (φ = 0.9789) and multiplicative seasonality. The Ljung-Box test gives p = 3.13e-09 (< 0.05), so the residuals are not white noise, and the ACF shows remaining autocorrelation at short and seasonal lags (12, 24). In-sample, ETS leaves information in the residuals and is inferior to SARIMA in this respect. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ets_forecast <- forecast(ets_auto, h = h + 36) autoplot(ets_forecast) + autolayer(ip_test, series = "Test data") + labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![ETS forecast against the test data](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-ets-forecast-1.png){#fig-ets-forecast width=768} ::: ::: 1. ETS reproduces the seasonal pattern but slightly underestimates the level over the test period. 2. The damped trend stabilises the central path and prevents unrealistic long-run growth. 3. The prediction intervals widen more slowly than for SARIMA: by Apr 2028 the upper 95% bound is 176.8, compared with 316.9 for SARIMA. ## Holt-Winters ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hw_add <- hw(ip_train, seasonal = "additive", h = h + 36) hw_mult <- hw(ip_train, seasonal = "multiplicative", h = h + 36) hw_lo95 <- hw_add$lower[, "95%"] hw_first_negative <- time(hw_lo95)[which(hw_lo95 < 0)[1]] data.frame( Model = c("Additive", "Multiplicative"), AIC = round(c(hw_add$model$aic, hw_mult$model$aic), 2), `RMSE (train)` = round(c(accuracy(hw_add)[, "RMSE"], accuracy(hw_mult)[, "RMSE"]), 4), alpha = round(c(hw_add$model$par["alpha"], hw_mult$model$par["alpha"]), 4), check.names = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Model | AIC| RMSE (train)| alpha| |:--------------|-------:|------------:|------:| |Additive | 1705.07| 0.7760| 0.9216| |Multiplicative | 1847.54| 0.9614| 0.4711|
::: ::: 1. The additive model fits better in-sample than the multiplicative one, with a lower AIC and a lower training RMSE. 2. α = 0.9216 in the additive model means the level reacts strongly to the most recent shocks. 3. Limitation: in the long-run forecast of the additive model, the lower 95% bound falls below zero from Nov 2023. This shows a weakness of classic additive structures on series in levels, compared with log-SARIMA. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hw_lb <- checkresiduals(hw_add) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ljung-Box test data: Residuals from Holt-Winters' additive method Q* = 107.62, df = 24, p-value = 1.464e-12 Model df: 0. Total lags used: 24 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residual diagnostics, additive Holt-Winters](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-hw-resid-1.png){#fig-hw-resid width=768} ::: ::: The Ljung-Box test gives p = 1.46e-12 (< 0.05): the residuals are not white noise, with large dependencies at the seasonal lags (12, 24, 36). Holt-Winters makes the seasonal component too rigid and does not remove the seasonal memory of the index; in-sample it is clearly inferior to SARIMA. ## Seasonal naive benchmark ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} naive_model <- snaive(ip_train, h = h + 36) autoplot(naive_model) + autolayer(ip_test, series = "Test data") + labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Seasonal naive forecast against the test data](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-snaive-1.png){#fig-snaive width=768} ::: ::: The seasonal naive forecast repeats the last observed seasonal cycle with a flat trend. It captures the monthly pattern but cannot adapt to changes in the trend, and its intervals are wide. It is the basic benchmark that more complex models must beat. ## Model comparison Forecasts were produced for `h + 36` months; only the first `h` months are compared with the test data. ::: {#tbl-accuracy .cell tbl-cap='Forecast accuracy on the test set (Jul 2016 to Apr 2025)'} ```{.r .cell-code} sarima_trim <- sarima_real$mean[1:h] ets_trim <- ets_forecast$mean[1:h] hw_trim <- hw_add$mean[1:h] naive_trim <- naive_model$mean[1:h] acc_table <- rbind( SARIMA = accuracy(sarima_trim, ip_test)[1, ], ETS = accuracy(ets_trim, ip_test)[1, ], HOLT_WINTERS = accuracy(hw_trim, ip_test)[1, ], SNAIVE = accuracy(naive_trim, ip_test)[1, ] ) round(acc_table, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ME RMSE MAE MPE MAPE ACF1 Theil's U SARIMA 0.1164 2.9259 1.7870 0.0228 1.8376 0.8183 1.3291 ETS 6.0648 6.9336 6.4773 5.9659 6.4523 0.8404 2.9332 HOLT_WINTERS 7.0010 8.2455 7.4029 6.9009 7.3754 0.8883 3.4925 SNAIVE 0.6704 3.1476 2.2613 0.5816 2.3026 0.7934 1.3995 ``` ::: ::: 1. SARIMA has the smallest errors: RMSE = 2.9259 and MAPE = 1.84%. 2. ETS (MAPE = 6.45%) and Holt-Winters (MAPE = 7.38%) systematically underestimate the test data. 3. SARIMA also beats the seasonal naive benchmark (MAPE = 2.3%). ### Diebold-Mariano test ::: {#tbl-dm .cell tbl-cap='Diebold-Mariano tests'} ```{.r .cell-code} e_sarima <- as.numeric(ip_test) - as.numeric(sarima_trim) e_ets <- as.numeric(ip_test) - as.numeric(ets_trim) e_hw <- as.numeric(ip_test) - as.numeric(hw_trim) dm_ets <- dm.test(e_sarima, e_ets, alternative = "two.sided", h = 1, power = 2) dm_hw <- dm.test(e_sarima, e_hw, alternative = "two.sided", h = 1, power = 2) data.frame( Comparison = c("SARIMA vs ETS", "SARIMA vs Holt-Winters"), `DM statistic` = round(c(dm_ets$statistic, dm_hw$statistic), 3), `p-value` = c(dm_ets$p.value, dm_hw$p.value), check.names = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Comparison | DM statistic| p-value| |:----------------------|------------:|-------:| |SARIMA vs ETS | -10.894| 0| |SARIMA vs Holt-Winters | -10.201| 0|
::: ::: In both comparisons the p-value is far below 0.05, so the null hypothesis of equal forecast accuracy is rejected. The negative DM statistics (-10.894 and -10.201) mean that the SARIMA errors are significantly smaller than those of the competing models. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} to_test_ts <- function(x) ts(x[1:h], start = start(ip_test), frequency = 12) autoplot(ip_ts, series = "Actual") + autolayer(to_test_ts(sarima_real$mean), series = "SARIMA", linewidth = 1) + autolayer(to_test_ts(ets_forecast$mean), series = "ETS", linewidth = 1) + autolayer(to_test_ts(hw_add$mean), series = "Holt-Winters", linewidth = 1) + autolayer(to_test_ts(naive_model$mean), series = "Seasonal naive", linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Forecasts over the test period](univariate_files/figure-html/fig-comparison-1.png){#fig-comparison width=768} ::: ::: The chart is consistent with the accuracy table and the Diebold-Mariano tests. SARIMA follows the level and the fluctuations of the actual series closely, around 100 index points. ETS and Holt-Winters drift downwards and underestimate the series, which explains their large errors. The seasonal naive forecast does reasonably well thanks to its flat trend but does not adapt to the dynamics of the series.
